items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S8026

SPONSOR: KAMINSKY
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the environmental conservation law, in relation to the
regulation of mining and the reclamation of mines within counties with a
population of one million or more which draw their primary source of
drinking water for a majority of county residents from a designated sole
source aquifer; and to repeal certain provisions of such law relating
thereto

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

Residents on Long Island draw their primary source of drinking water
from a federally designated sole source aquifer. Proactive measures must
be taken to protect this precious natural resource from potential sourc-
es of contamination.

This legislation implements Suffolk County Grand Jury recommendations to
better protect water quality by providing new regulatory authority to
counties and local governments over mining activities and eliminating
current permit exemptions for mining relating to construction activities
and agricultural activities. The legislation would apply only within
counties with a population of one million or more which draw their
primary source of drinking water for a majority of county residents from
a designated sole source aquifer (Long Island).

The authority for local governments on Long Island over mining would be
concurrent with existing oversight provided by the state.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section 1 of this bill repeals Section 23-2703 of the Environmental
Conservation Law and replaces it with a new Section 23-2703 which
provides:

 *Subdivision 1- finds that mining must be compatible with the
protection of water quality within counties with a population of one
million or more which draw their primary source of drinking water for a
majority of county residents from a designated sole source aquifer(Long
Island).

 *Subdivision 2- maintains all existing exceptions to state pre-exemp-
tion where local governments may currently act to regulate mining.
 *Subdivision 3- adds additional preemption exceptions for the
protection water quality by authorizing the regulation of mining by
local governments within counties with a population of one million or
more which draw their primary source of drinking water for a majority of
county residents from a designated sole source aquifer (Long Island).
Long Island local governments may regulate mining by enacting local laws
for the purpose of protection water quality and public health, includ-
ing: (a) prohibiting mining on properties where it would be inconsistent
with water quality protection and public health, (b) authorizing ground-
water monitoring of mining sites, (c) prohibiting mining on contaminated
sites where contamination exceeds state or federal water quality stand-
ards, (d) regulating or prohibiting of the co-location of mines with
facilities that receive and process waste (e) eliminating mining sites
which are non-conforming under zoning regulations, where it is necessary
to protect water quality, (f) regulating mining reclamation, (g) any
other regulation necessary to protect water quality.

 *Subdivision 4 provides that no state agency could process or approve
an application for sand mining on Long Island (a) where local laws,
including zoning, prohibit mining at the mining site or (b) where the
local government has denied a permit for mining at the site.  Addi-
tionally, it provides that no state agency could approve a mining permit
until it has been approved by local government. This provision applies
to all permits, including new permits, renewals, and expansions on
existing sites.

Section 2 amends subdivision 8 of Section 23-2705 of the Environmental
Conservation Law to repeal the mining permit exemptions for the mining
of sand on Long Island for the purposes of construction activities and
agricultural activities.

Section 3 amends paragraph (b) of subdivision 3 of section 23-2711 of
the Environmental Conservation Law and provides that local government
determinations and local laws relating to mining activities pursuant to
this act could not be pre-empted but would be binding upon the Depart-
ment of Environmental Conservation.

Section 4 provides for judicial review of local government determi-
nations in accordance to article seventy-eight of the civil practice law
and rules.

Section 5 is the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Inadequate regulation of mining presents a threat to the drinking water
supply in locations like Long Island which draw their primary source of
drinking water from a designated sole source aquifer. One example is the
Sand Land mining operation in the Town of Southampton.  Sand Land is
located in a residential area. It is also within a Special Groundwater
Protection Area designated by the State of New York. Both surface water
and groundwater have been contaminated on the site far exceeding state
and federal drinking water standards.  The Suffolk County Health Depart-
ment conducted an investigation and released a report in June 2018 docu-
menting the level of contamination at the site.

The report indicated that serious contamination of groundwater has
occurred with numerous contaminants including chemicals, radiation and
heavy metals. The Suffolk County Health Department found iron, manga-
nese, thallium, sodium, nitrate, ammonia, and radioactivity in the deep-
est part of the underground aquifer below the sand mine. Iron was found
at concentrations over 200 times the drinking water standard. Manganese
was found at concentrations nearly 100 times the standard.

Subsequently, a Grand Jury was empaneled in Suffolk County between July
18, 2018 and August 2, 2019 regarding illegal dumping and sand mining.
Over that time, testimony was heard, and evidence was reviewed which
highlighted the importance of protecting the environment of Suffolk
County from illegal dumping and sand mining.

With regard to sand mining, the Grand Jury made findings that additional
regulation over mining activities was necessary within counties with a
population of one million or more which draw their primary source of
drinking water for a majority of county residents from a designated sole
source aquifer in order to protect the region's water quality.

This legislation implements the recommendations of that Grand Jury
report including:

 (a) a legislative declaration of policy that fosters and encourages the
development of an economically and stable mining industry that is
compatible with the protection of water quality on Long Island.

 (b) new regulatory authority to counties and other local governments
over mining activities for the purposes of protecting water quality.
This authority would be in addition to the existing oversight provided
by the state.

 (c) the repeal of mining permit exemptions for the purposes of mining
related to construction and agricultural activities.

 (d) The applicability of this law would be limited to counties with a
population of one million or more which draw their primary source of
drinking water for a majority of county residents from a designated sole
source aquifer.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None to the State.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

summary: Provides for the regulation of mining and the reclamation of mines within counties with a population of one million or more which draw their primary source of drinking water for a majority of county residents from a designated sole source aquifer.
